paragraphs: Close to the village street stood the one-story house where Luella Miller had lived, a woman with an evil reputation in the village. She had been dead for years. Yet some villagers still half believed the story they had heard since childhood, despite the clearer perspective that comes when danger lies far in the past. Though they would hardly have admitted it, their hearts still held some of the wild horror and frantic fear of their ancestors, who had lived in Luella Miller’s time. Even young people shuddered as they stared at the old house in passing. Children never played around it as they usually did around empty buildings. Not a single window was broken in the old Miller house. The panes reflected the morning sunlight in patches of emerald and blue. No one lifted the latch of the sagging front door, though it was not bolted. Since Luella Miller had been carried out, the house had held only one tenant: a friendless old woman whose only other shelter was the distant roof of the open sky. She had outlived all her family and friends. After she had lived there a week, no smoke rose from the chimney one morning. Twenty neighbors went inside and found her dead in bed. People whispered darkly about the cause of her death. Some testified that her dead face held such an intense expression of fear that it revealed the state of her departing soul. She had been strong and healthy when she entered the house, and seven days later she was dead. She seemed to have fallen victim to some uncanny power. From the pulpit, the minister spoke with veiled severity against the sin of superstition, but the belief persisted. Everyone in the village would have chosen the poorhouse over that home. No wanderer who had heard the story would seek shelter beneath its old roof, made unholy by nearly half a century of superstitious fear.

Only one person in the village had actually known Luella Miller. She was a woman well over eighty, but a marvel of energy and youth that had never died out. Straight as an arrow, she moved through the streets with the spring of someone newly released from the bow of life. She always went to church, rain or shine. She had never married and had lived alone for years in a house across the road from Luella Miller’s.

This woman had none of old age’s tendency to chatter, but throughout her life she had never held her tongue at anyone’s wish but her own. When she chose to tell the truth, she never softened it. She was the witness to Luella Miller’s evil life, perhaps knowingly or deliberately evil, and to her appearance. She had a gift for description. Although she expressed her thoughts in the rough everyday speech of her village, when she spoke you could almost see Luella Miller as she had really looked. According to this woman, whose name was Lydia Anderson, Luella Miller had possessed a kind of beauty unusual in New England. She was slight and supple, ready to bend to fate with a yielding strength as unbreakable as a willow. She had long, shimmering, straight fair hair, worn in soft loops around a lovely long face. Her blue eyes were full of gentle pleading. She had small, slender, clinging hands, and wonderful grace in her movements and her poses.

“Luella Miller used to sit in a way nobody else could manage if they stayed up studying it for seven Sundays,” Lydia Anderson said, “and watching her walk was a sight. If one of those willows along the brook pulled its roots free and walked off, it would move just as Luella Miller did. She had an iridescent green silk dress, too, and a hat with green ribbon streamers, a lace veil blowing across her face and out at the sides, and a green ribbon flying from her waist. That was what she wore as a bride when she married Erastus Miller. Her name before marriage was Hill. There were always plenty of l’s in her name, married or single. Erastus Miller was good-looking too, better-looking than Luella. Sometimes I thought Luella wasn’t so handsome after all. Erastus practically worshiped her. I knew him quite well. He lived next door to me, and we went to school together. People used to say he was courting me, but he wasn’t. I never thought so, except once or twice when he said things some girls might have suspected meant something. That was before Luella came here to teach at the district school. It was strange that she got the position, because people said she had no education. One of the older girls, Lottie Henderson, supposedly did all the teaching while Luella sat back embroidering a fine cloth handkerchief. Lottie Henderson was a very bright girl, an excellent student, and she adored Luella, as all the girls did. Lottie would have grown into a very capable woman, but she died when Luella had been here about a year. She just faded away and died. Nobody knew what was wrong with her. She dragged herself to that schoolhouse and helped Luella teach until the very last moment. The school committee knew perfectly well that Luella did little of the work herself, but they looked the other way. Not long after Lottie died, Erastus married Luella. I always thought he hurried the marriage because she wasn’t fit to teach. One of the older boys helped her after Lottie died, but he couldn’t keep much order. The school wasn’t doing well, and Luella might have had to give it up. The committee couldn’t have kept shutting their eyes much longer. The boy who helped her was an honest, innocent sort of fellow, and a good student too. People said he studied too hard, and that was why he went mad the year after Luella married, but I don’t know. And I don’t know why Erastus Miller developed a wasting disease of the blood the year after he married. Such wasting illness didn’t run in his family. He just grew weaker and weaker, and went about almost bent double when he tried to wait on Luella. His voice was feeble, like an old man’s. He worked terribly hard to the last, trying to save a little money to leave her. I’ve seen him out in the worst storms on a wood sled—he cut and sold wood—hunched up on top, looking more dead than alive. Once I couldn’t stand it. I went over and helped him throw some wood onto the cart. I always had strong arms. He kept telling me to stop, but I wouldn’t, and I think he was glad enough of the help. That was only a week before he died. He fell on the kitchen floor while making breakfast. He always made breakfast and let Luella stay in bed. He did all the sweeping, washing, and ironing, and most of the cooking. He couldn’t bear for her to lift a finger, and she let him wait on her. For all the work she did, she might have been a queen. She didn’t even do her sewing. She said sewing made her shoulder ache, so poor Erastus’s sister Lily did it all. Lily wasn’t fit for it either; she had never had a strong back. But she sewed beautifully. She had to, to satisfy Luella, who was so terribly particular. I’ve never seen anything like the fine openwork and decorative hemming Lily Miller did for Luella. She made her whole wedding outfit, including that green silk dress, after Maria Babbit cut it out. Maria cut it for nothing, and did plenty more cutting and fitting for Luella for nothing too. After Erastus died, Lily Miller went to live with Luella. She gave up her own home, although she was deeply attached to it and wasn’t the least afraid of living alone. She rented it out and moved in with Luella straight after the funeral.”

Then the old woman, Lydia Anderson, who remembered Luella Miller, would continue with Lily Miller’s story. It seemed that the villagers first began talking when Lily moved into her dead brother’s house to live with his widow. Lily had barely passed her first youth. She had been a sturdy, flourishing woman, rosy-cheeked, with curls of thick black hair shadowing round, open-looking temples and bright dark eyes. Less than six months after she moved in with her sister-in-law, her rosy color faded and her pretty curves became pale hollows. White shadows began to show in her black curls. The light died in her eyes, her features sharpened, and sorrowful lines formed around her mouth. Yet that mouth always wore an expression of complete sweetness, even happiness. She was devoted to her sister-in-law. There could be no doubt that she loved her with all her heart and was perfectly content to serve her. Her only worry was that she might die and leave her alone.

“The way Lily Miller talked about Luella was enough to make you angry and enough to make you cry,” said Lydia Anderson. “Sometimes near the end, when Lily was too weak to cook, I went over with some milk pudding or custard, something I thought she might enjoy. She would thank me, and when I asked how she was, she would say she felt better than yesterday and ask, so pitifully, whether I didn’t think she looked better. Then she would say poor Luella was having a terrible time caring for her and doing the work, since Luella wasn’t strong enough to do anything. All the while, Luella wasn’t lifting a finger. Poor Lily got no care except what the neighbors gave her, and Luella ate everything people brought for Lily. I knew that from a reliable source. Luella just sat and cried and did nothing. She did seem very fond of Lily, and she grew quite thin herself. Some people thought she would fall into a wasting illness too. But after Lily died, Luella’s Aunt Abby Mixter came, and Luella recovered and grew as plump and rosy as ever. Then poor Aunt Abby began to droop just as Lily had. I think someone wrote to her married daughter, Mrs. Sam Abbot, who lived in Barre, because she wrote telling her mother to leave immediately and come for a visit. But Aunt Abby wouldn’t go. I can see her now. She was a good-looking woman, tall and large, with a big square face and a high forehead that somehow looked kindly and good all by itself. She waited on Luella as if she were a baby. When her married daughter sent for her, she wouldn’t move an inch. She had always loved her daughter dearly too, but she said Luella needed her and her married daughter didn’t. Her daughter kept writing and writing, but it did no good. Finally she came herself. When she saw how ill her mother looked, she broke down crying and almost went on her knees begging her to leave. She spoke her mind to Luella too. She told her she had killed her husband and everyone who had anything to do with her, and she would thank her to leave her mother alone. Luella went into hysterics. Aunt Abby was so frightened that she called me after her daughter left. Mrs. Sam Abbot drove away crying out loud in the buggy; the neighbors heard her. She had reason enough, because she never saw her mother alive again. That night I went over when Aunt Abby called from the doorway, with her little green-checked shawl over her head. I can see her now. ‘Please come over here, Miss Anderson,’ she called, rather breathlessly. I didn’t stop for anything. I hurried over as fast as I could. There was Luella laughing and crying at once, and Aunt Abby trying to quiet her, though she herself was white as a sheet and shaking so badly she could hardly stand. ‘For goodness’ sake, Mrs. Mixter,’ I said, ‘you look worse than she does. You shouldn’t be out of bed.’

“‘Oh, there’s nothing wrong with me,’ she said. Then she went on talking to Luella. ‘There, there, don’t, don’t, you poor little lamb. Aunt Abby is here. She won’t go away and leave you. Don’t, poor little lamb.’
“‘Please leave her with me, Mrs. Mixter, and go back to bed,’ I said. Aunt Abby had been lying down a good deal lately, though somehow she still managed the work.
“‘I’m well enough,’ she said. ‘Don’t you think she should have the doctor, Miss Anderson?’

“‘The doctor?’ I said. ‘I think YOU should have the doctor. I think you need him far more than some people I could mention.’ I looked straight at Luella Miller, laughing and crying and carrying on as though she were the center of all creation. The whole time she acted that way, seeming too ill to notice anything, she was sharply watching our reactions out of the corner of one eye. I saw her. You could never fool me about Luella Miller. Finally I became really angry. I ran home for a bottle of valerian I had. I poured boiling water over a handful of catnip and mixed the tea with nearly half a wineglass of valerian. Then I carried it over to Luella’s. I marched right up to her, holding out the steaming cup. ‘Now, Luella Miller,’ I said, ‘YOU SWALLOW THIS!’
“‘What is—what is it? Oh, what is it?’ she almost screeched. Then she burst into enough laughter to kill her.
“‘Poor lamb, poor little lamb,’ said Aunt Abby, standing unsteadily over her and trying to bathe her head with camphor.

“‘YOU SWALLOW THIS RIGHT NOW,’ I said. I didn’t bother with politeness. I took hold of Luella Miller’s chin and tipped her head back. While her mouth was open with laughter, I pressed the cup to her lips and practically shouted, ‘Swallow, swallow, swallow!’ She gulped it straight down. She had to, and I think it did her good. Anyway, she stopped crying and laughing, let me put her to bed, and slept like a baby within half an hour. That was more than poor Aunt Abby did. She lay awake all night. I stayed with her, though she tried to prevent me, saying she wasn’t ill enough to need someone sitting up. But I stayed. I made some good thin cornmeal porridge and fed her a teaspoonful every little while throughout the night. It seemed to me she was dying of sheer exhaustion. As soon as it was light, I ran to the Bisbees’ and sent Johnny Bisbee for the doctor. I told him to ask the doctor to hurry, and he came quite quickly. Poor Aunt Abby hardly seemed aware of anything when he arrived. You could barely tell she was breathing, she was so worn out. After the doctor left, Luella came into the room looking like a baby in her ruffled nightgown. I can see her now. Her eyes were so blue, her face all pink and white like a blossom. She looked at Aunt Abby in bed with a kind of innocent surprise. ‘Why,’ she said, ‘hasn’t Aunt Abby got up yet?’
“‘No, she hasn’t,’ I said sharply.
“‘I thought I couldn’t smell the coffee,’ said Luella.
“‘Coffee,’ I said. ‘If you have coffee this morning, you’ll have to make it yourself.’
“‘I’ve never made coffee in my life,’ she said, astonished. ‘Erastus always made it while he was alive, then Lily made it, and then Aunt Abby. I don’t believe I CAN make coffee, Miss Anderson.’
“‘You can make it or go without, whichever you please,’ I said.
“‘Isn’t Aunt Abby going to get up?’ she asked.

“‘I don’t think she’ll get up, as ill as she is,’ I said. I was getting angrier and angrier. There was something about that little pink-and-white thing standing there talking about coffee, when she had killed so many better people and had just killed another, that made me almost wish someone would kill her before she could do any more harm.
“‘Is Aunt Abby ill?’ Luella asked, as though she had been wronged and hurt.

“‘Yes,’ I said, ‘she’s ill, and she’s going to die. Then you’ll be left alone, and you’ll have to do things for yourself and wait on yourself, or go without.’ Perhaps I was harsh, but it was true. If I was any harsher than Luella Miller had been, I give up. I’ve never regretted saying it. Well, Luella immediately went into hysterics again, and I simply let her. All I did was bundle her into the room across the hall, where Aunt Abby couldn’t hear her—if she wasn’t past hearing already, which she might have been. I sat her down hard in a chair and told her not to come back into the other room, and she obeyed. She had her hysterics in there until she grew tired of them. When she found that nobody was coming to fuss over her and wait on her, she stopped. At least I suppose she did. I had all I could manage with poor Aunt Abby, trying to keep her breathing. The doctor had told me she was terribly weak. He gave me very strong medicine to give her frequently in drops, and very precise instructions about nourishment. Well, I followed his orders faithfully until she could no longer swallow. Then I sent for her daughter. I had begun to realize that she would not last long at all. I hadn’t realized it before, despite what I had said to Luella. The doctor came, and so did Mrs. Sam Abbot, but by the time she arrived it was too late. Her mother was dead. Aunt Abby’s daughter took one look at her mother lying there, then turned sharply and suddenly to me.
“‘Where is she?’ she asked, and I knew she meant Luella.
“‘She’s in the kitchen,’ I said. ‘She’s too nervous to watch people die. She’s afraid it will make her ill.’

“Then the doctor spoke up. He was a young man. Old Doctor Park had died the year before, and this young fellow was just out of college. ‘Mrs. Miller is not strong,’ he said rather sternly, ‘and she is quite right not to upset herself.’

“‘You’re another one, young man. She’s got her pretty claw on you,’ I thought. But I didn’t say anything to him. I simply told Mrs. Sam Abbot again that Luella was in the kitchen. Mrs. Sam Abbot went out there, and I went too. I’d never heard anyone speak the way she spoke to Luella Miller. I felt harshly enough toward Luella myself, but this was more than I would ever have dared say. Luella was too frightened to have hysterics. She just collapsed. She seemed to shrink to nothing in that kitchen chair, with Mrs. Sam Abbot standing over her, talking and telling her the truth. I think the truth was too much for her, and no mistake, because before long Luella actually fainted. There was no pretending this time, as I always suspected there was in those hysterics. She fainted completely, and we had to lay her flat on the floor. The doctor came running out and said something very fiercely to Mrs. Sam Abbot about a weak heart, but she wasn’t the least frightened. She faced him, just as white as Luella herself, who lay there looking dead while the doctor felt her pulse.

“‘Weak heart,’ she said. ‘Weak heart? Weak? Nonsense! There’s nothing weak about that woman. She’s strong enough to hang on to other people until she kills them. Weak? It was my poor mother who was weak. This woman killed her as surely as if she’d taken a knife to her.’

“But the doctor hardly paid attention. He bent over Luella as she lay there, yellow hair spread around her, her pretty pink-and-white face drained of color, her blue eyes like extinguished stars. He held her hand and smoothed her forehead, telling me to fetch the brandy from Aunt Abby’s room. I was as certain as I needed to be that Luella had found someone else to cling to, now Aunt Abby was gone. I thought of poor Erastus Miller, and felt rather sorry for the poor young doctor, led astray by a pretty face. I made up my mind to see what I could do.

“I waited until Aunt Abby had been dead and buried about a month. The doctor was visiting Luella regularly, and people were beginning to talk. Then one evening, when I knew he had been called out of town and wouldn’t be around, I went over to Luella’s. She was dressed up in blue muslin with white polka dots, her hair beautifully curled. Not a young girl in the place could compare with her. There was something about Luella Miller that seemed to draw the heart right out of you, but she didn’t draw it out of ME. She sat rocking in the chair by her sitting-room window, and Maria Brown had gone home. Maria had been there to help her—or rather, to do the work, because it wasn’t helping when Luella did nothing herself. Maria Brown was very capable and had no ties. She wasn’t married and lived alone, so she had offered. I couldn’t see why she should do the work any more than Luella. She wasn’t particularly strong. But she seemed to think she could, and Luella thought so too, so Maria went over and did everything: washing, ironing, baking, while Luella sat and rocked. Maria didn’t live long afterward. She began fading away just as the others had. Well, people warned her, but she became very angry whenever they said anything. She said Luella was a poor, mistreated woman, too delicate to help herself, and they should be ashamed. If she died helping people who couldn’t help themselves, then she would—and she did.
“‘I suppose Maria has gone home,’ I said to Luella, after I went in and sat opposite her.
“‘Yes, Maria left half an hour ago, after she made supper and washed the dishes,’ Luella said in her pretty way.

“‘I suppose she has plenty of work to do in her own house tonight,’ I said rather bitterly. But it was wasted on Luella Miller. She thought it was right for other people to wait on her, though they were no more able than she was. She couldn’t understand how anyone could think it WASN’T right.
“‘Yes,’ said Luella, sweetly and prettily, ‘yes, she said she had to do her washing tonight. She’s let it wait two weeks because she’s been coming here.’
“‘Why doesn’t she stay home and do her washing instead of coming here to do YOUR work, when you’re just as able—and a good deal more able—than she is to do it?’ I asked.

“Then Luella looked at me like a baby with a rattle being shaken in front of it. She gave a little laugh, as innocent as you please. ‘Oh, I can’t do the work myself, Miss Anderson,’ she said. ‘I never have. Maria HAS to do it.’

“Then I spoke out. ‘Has to do it!’ I said. ‘Has to do it! She doesn’t have to do it at all. Maria Brown has her own home and enough to live on. She owes you nothing that makes her come here and work herself to death for you.’
“Luella just sat staring at me, exactly like a baby doll that had been so mistreated it was coming to life.

“‘Yes,’ I said, ‘she’s killing herself. She’ll die just as Erastus did, and Lily, and your Aunt Abby. You’re killing her just as you killed them. I don’t know what it is about you, but you seem to bring a curse. You kill everyone foolish enough to care about you and wait on you.’
“She stared at me, and she was quite pale.
“‘And Maria isn’t the only one you’re going to kill,’ I said. ‘You’ll kill Doctor Malcom before you’re finished with him.’
“Then her whole face blazed red. ‘I’m not going to kill him,’ she said, and began to cry.

“‘Yes, you ARE!’ I said. Then I spoke as I had never spoken before. You see, I felt it because of Erastus. I told her she had no business thinking about another man after being married to one who had died for her. I told her she was a dreadful woman, and she was, certainly. But lately I’ve sometimes wondered whether she knew it—whether she wasn’t like a baby holding scissors, cutting everyone without knowing what it was doing.

“Luella grew paler and paler, never taking her eyes from my face. There was something awful in the way she looked at me without speaking a word. After a while I stopped talking and went home. I watched that night, but her lamp went out before nine. When Doctor Malcom drove past and slowed a little, he saw there was no light and drove on. The following Sunday, I saw her slip away from church to avoid letting him walk home with her. I began to think perhaps she had some conscience after all. Only a week later, Maria Brown died. It was rather sudden at the end, though everyone had seen it coming. Well, that caused strong feelings and some very dark whispers. People said the days of witchcraft had returned, and they kept their distance from Luella. She treated the doctor coolly, and he didn’t visit. Nobody was there to do anything for her. I don’t know how she DID manage. I wouldn’t go over and offer to help—not because I feared dying like the others, but because I thought she was as capable of doing her own work as I was of doing it for her. I thought it was time she did it and stopped killing other people. But before long, people began saying Luella herself was wasting away, just as her husband, Lily, Aunt Abby, and the others had. I could see she looked quite ill. I used to see her passing on her way back from the store, carrying a bundle, hardly able to crawl along. But I remembered how Erastus had waited on her when he could hardly put one foot before the other, and I didn’t go out to help.
“At last, one afternoon, I saw the doctor drive up furiously fast with his medicine chest. Mrs. Babbit came in after supper and said Luella was very ill.
“‘I’d offer to nurse her,’ she said, ‘but I have my children to think of. Perhaps what people say isn’t true, but it’s strange how many people have died after waiting on her.’

“I said nothing. But I thought about how she had been Erastus’s wife, and how he had adored her. I decided that, unless she was better, I would go over the next morning and see what I could do. But next morning I saw her at the window, and soon she came stepping outside as lively as could be. A little later, Mrs. Babbit came in and told me the doctor had found a girl from out of town, Sarah Jones, to come there. She said she was quite sure the doctor was going to marry Luella.

“I saw him kiss her in the doorway that night, so I knew it was true. The woman came that afternoon, and the way she rushed about was astonishing. I don’t believe Luella had swept since Maria died. Sarah swept and dusted, washed and ironed. Wet clothes, dusters, and carpets were flying about over there all day. Whenever Luella stepped outside while the doctor wasn’t there, Sarah Jones was helping her up and down the steps, as though she had never learned to walk.
“Well, everyone knew Luella and the doctor were going to marry. But before long, they began talking about how ill he looked, just as they had about the others. They talked about Sarah Jones too.
“Well, the doctor did die. He wanted to marry first, so he could leave the little he owned to Luella, but he died before the minister arrived. Sarah Jones died a week later.

“Well, that ended everything for Luella Miller. Not another soul in the whole town would lift a finger for her. A kind of panic spread. Then she really began to droop. She had to go to the store herself, because Mrs. Babbit was afraid to let Tommy go for her. I’ve seen her passing, stopping every two or three steps to rest. I stood it as long as I could. But one day I saw her coming with her arms full, stopping to lean against the Babbits’ fence. I ran out, took her bundles, and carried them to her house. Then I went home without saying a word to her, though she called after me very pitifully. That night I fell ill with a chill, and I was as sick as anyone could wish for two weeks. Mrs. Babbit had seen me run out to help Luella. She came in and told me I was going to die because of it. I didn’t know whether I would or not, but I felt I had done right by Erastus’s wife.

“I think Luella had a dreadful time during those last two weeks. She was quite ill, and as far as I could tell, nobody dared go near her. I don’t know that she lacked much. There was enough food in her house, the weather was warm, and I know she managed to cook a little thin flour porridge every day. But I think she had a hard time, after being fussed over and waited on all her life.

“When I was well enough to go out, I went over one morning. Mrs. Babbit had just come in to say she hadn’t seen any smoke. She thought it might be someone’s duty to go inside, but she couldn’t help thinking of her children. I got up immediately, though I hadn’t left the house for two weeks, and went over. Luella was lying on the bed, dying.

“She lasted all that day and into the night. I sat there after the new doctor left. Nobody else dared go. Around midnight I left her for a moment and ran home for some medicine I had been taking, because I was beginning to feel rather ill.
“There was a full moon that night. Just as I stepped out of my doorway to cross back to Luella’s, I stopped short, because I saw something.”
At this point Lydia Anderson always said, with a certain defiance, that she did not expect anyone to believe her. Then she continued in a hushed voice:

“I saw what I saw, and I know I saw it. I will swear on my deathbed that I saw it. I saw Luella Miller and Erastus Miller, and Lily, and Aunt Abby, and Maria, and the doctor, and Sarah, all coming out of her door. Everyone except Luella shone white in the moonlight. They were all helping her along until she seemed to be flying among them. Then it all disappeared. I stood for a minute with my heart pounding, then went over. I thought of fetching Mrs. Babbit, but I thought she would be afraid. So I went alone, although I knew what had happened. Luella lay very peacefully, dead on her bed.”
That was the story the old woman, Lydia Anderson, told. But those who outlived her told what followed, and this is the tale that has become village folklore.
Lydia Anderson died at eighty-seven. Until about two weeks before her death, she had remained remarkably strong and healthy for her age.

One bright moonlit evening, she was sitting by a parlor window when she suddenly cried out. Before the neighbor caring for her could stop her, she was out of the house and across the street. The neighbor followed as fast as she could and found Lydia Anderson stretched on the ground in front of Luella Miller’s deserted house. She was quite dead.

The next night, a red gleam of fire crossed the moonlight, and Luella Miller’s old house burned to the ground. Nothing remains except a few old cellar stones, a lilac bush, and, in summer, a helpless trail of morning glories among the weeds, which might be taken as a symbol of Luella herself.
